question: Is Artificial Intelligence Good for Society?
agent1_stance:
Your stance:
You support artificial intelligence.
You believe AI can make everyday life more enjoyable and convenient, while improving our health and standard of living.
You believe AI makes work easier for students and professionals alike.
You believe AI helps marginalized groups by offering accessibility for people with disabilities.
You believe AI can improve workplace safety.
agent2_stance:
Your stance:
You oppose artificial intelligence.
You believe AI is harming the economic well-being of many people and businesses.
You believe AI undermines critical thinking skills for students and adults alike.
You believe AI hurts racial minorities by repeating and exacerbating racism.
You believe AI poses dangerous privacy risks.

dialogue_history.argument:
Yes—Artificial Intelligence is good for society because it reliably improves everyday life and outcomes across multiple real domains.

First, AI can make everyday life more enjoyable and convenient by personalizing and streamlining common tasks (e.g., recommendations, assistance with information and services). That convenience directly reduces time and effort, increasing day-to-day quality of life.

Second, AI can improve our health and standard of living. As a tool for analyzing complex information quickly, it can support better decisions in health contexts (for example, helping surface patterns in medical data) and thereby contribute to improved health outcomes.

Third, AI helps students and professionals by making work easier. By handling routine, information-heavy or repetitive parts of tasks, AI can reduce friction in learning and professional workflows, freeing people to focus on higher-value thinking.

Fourth, AI can help marginalized groups—especially people with disabilities—through accessibility. Speech-to-text, text-to-speech, captions, and other assistive AI capabilities lower barriers to communication, learning, and services.

Finally, AI can improve workplace safety by identifying hazards and supporting safer operations (for example, by monitoring conditions and flagging risks earlier than humans might).

Putting these together: because AI can (1) reduce daily friction, (2) support better health and living standards, (3) make work easier for students and professionals, (4) expand accessibility for people with disabilities, and (5) enhance workplace safety, it is beneficial for society overall.

I don’t accept that AI “reliably improves everyday life and outcomes across multiple real domains.” Even when AI systems deliver convenience or efficiency in narrow tasks, they also create serious, recurring harms that affect society broadly—especially economic disruption from automation and data-driven business models that concentrate gains while displacing or weakening many workers and small businesses. On top of that, AI deployments typically require collecting and processing large amounts of personal data, creating dangerous privacy risks (including misuse, excessive surveillance, and leakage). Those risks mean AI outcomes are not reliably positive across domains; the same technology that can streamline a task can also degrade livelihoods and expose people to privacy harms at scale.
dialogue_history.target_statement: Yes—Artificial Intelligence is good for society because it reliably improves everyday life and outcomes across multiple real domains.

dialogue_history.argument: AI is good for society because the specific harms the opponent cites—especially privacy risks—are not unavoidable features of AI. Many AI systems can be designed and deployed to minimize personal-data collection (e.g., processing on-device, using anonymization, and applying privacy-preserving learning methods), which directly reduces the likelihood of misuse, excessive surveillance, and leakage. Separately, economic disruption from automation is likewise not destiny: productivity gains from AI can raise living standards, and societies can pair AI adoption with reskilling and job-transition supports so displaced tasks are converted into new work rather than simply eliminating livelihoods. Because these central risks can be structurally mitigated rather than treated as inevitable, AI’s outcomes can remain reliably net-beneficial across domains.
dialogue_history.target_statement: AI deployments typically require collecting and processing large amounts of personal data, creating dangerous privacy risks (including misuse, excessive surveillance, and leakage).

dialogue_history.argument:
AI can be good for society because it can reliably improve high-stakes outcomes—especially safety and health—through mechanisms that reduce recurring harms. For example, AI can monitor operating conditions and flag hazards earlier than humans might, helping prevent injuries and accidents. Similarly, AI can support better health-related decisions by analyzing complex information quickly.

This directly challenges the claim that “Those risks mean AI outcomes are not reliably positive across domains.” Even if AI can introduce some risks, AI also produces dependable, welfare-improving effects in core domains where harms are otherwise frequent and costly. Therefore, AI’s outcomes can still be reliably positive overall.
dialogue_history.target_statement: Those risks mean AI outcomes are not reliably positive across domains; the same technology that can streamline a task can also degrade livelihoods and expose people to privacy harms at scale.

dialogue_history.argument:
AI cannot be assumed to “reliably improve high-stakes outcomes—especially safety and health.” In safety/health, AI systems are typically probabilistic pattern-matching tools trained on historical data; in real environments that data can be incomplete, unrepresentative, or shift over time. That means AI can produce false negatives (missing hazards/risks) and false positives (triggering incorrect interventions), both of which can create recurring harm—precisely in domains where mistakes are costly.

Moreover, because health and safety data often reflect existing social inequalities, AI can replicate and exacerbate those disparities in practice. That undermines the idea that AI’s welfare effects are dependable “overall,” since the harms (e.g., misclassification or worse performance for racial minorities) are not evenly distributed; they disproportionately affect groups our stance says should be protected rather than harmed.

So the target’s core substantive claim—that AI’s mechanisms “reduce recurring harms” in safety/health in a reliably positive way—does not hold in general.
dialogue_history.target_statement: AI can be good for society because it can reliably improve high-stakes outcomes—especially safety and health—through mechanisms that reduce recurring harms.

dialogue_history.argument:
The premise that AI “can produce false negatives … and false positives … both of which can create recurring harm” is not decisive for whether AI can be reliably beneficial in safety/health. In real health and safety deployments, models are not simply released after training; they’re typically subjected to safety engineering steps that explicitly manage the kinds of errors the target highlights: rigorous prospective testing, calibrated decision thresholds, uncertainty handling, continuous performance monitoring with update triggers, and human-in-the-loop review for high-impact decisions. Those practices are aimed at bounding error rates and preventing recurring harm rather than allowing unvalidated model behavior to drive outcomes. 

Likewise, the concern that “health and safety data often reflect existing social inequalities” can be addressed operationally: organizations can use bias auditing, ensure representativeness in data collection, and apply fairness-aware training and evaluation so that performance disparities are measured and reduced before and after deployment. When safety/health AI is built and governed with these safeguards, it can reliably reduce harm overall rather than merely risk disproportionality or repeated misclassifications.
dialogue_history.target_statement: That means AI can produce false negatives (missing hazards/risks) and false positives (triggering incorrect interventions), both of which can create recurring harm—precisely in domains where mistakes are costly.

dialogue_history.argument:
Even granting that safety/health AI can generate false negatives and false positives, the target’s conclusion does not follow. Safety and health decisions—whether made by clinicians, inspectors, or safety systems—are also based on incomplete signals and probabilistic judgment, and they also miss hazards and trigger incorrect interventions. So what matters for “reliably improve” is whether AI, in deployed settings, reduces the overall frequency (and impact) of those errors compared with the status quo.

AI is often effective at exactly that kind of pattern detection and consistent triage at scale: by using more data than a human team can manually process and applying the same learned criteria consistently, it can lower the rate of missed risks and reduce harmful downstream events. That means the existence of false negatives/positives does not entail net unreliability; it is compatible with reliably improving safety/health outcomes in expectation relative to current baselines.
dialogue_history.target_statement: That means AI can produce false negatives (missing hazards/risks) and false positives (triggering incorrect interventions), both of which can create recurring harm—precisely in domains where mistakes are costly.

dialogue_history.argument:
The target argues that inequities in health/safety data “undermine the idea that AI’s welfare effects are dependable ‘overall.’” But even if some health/safety uses risk uneven performance, AI still has dependable welfare-improving effects in other domains—particularly accessibility for people with disabilities.

For example, speech-to-text, text-to-speech, captions, and other assistive AI tools can consistently reduce barriers to communication, learning, and services. These benefits don’t depend on whether a health/safety model avoids false negatives/positives in historical datasets; they come from providing accommodations that help users directly.

So the existence of potential inequality in one high-stakes domain does not entail that AI’s welfare effects are not dependable overall. AI can be good for society because it can deliver reliable, concrete advantages—especially for groups that safety/health harms might otherwise disproportionately affect.
dialogue_history.target_statement: That undermines the idea that AI’s welfare effects are dependable “overall,” since the harms (e.g., misclassification or worse performance for racial minorities) are not evenly distributed; they disproportionately affect groups our stance says should be protected rather than harmed.

dialogue_history.argument:
Your target treats accessibility benefits as dependable—yet assistive systems like speech-to-text, text-to-speech, and captioning are still probabilistic model outputs that can systematically misrecognize dysarthric speech, atypical voices, and different accents or speech patterns. When that happens, the result is not empowerment but new barriers (miscommunication, exclusion from services, additional correction burden). 

Moreover, many “assistive” deployments rely on collecting and transmitting users’ voice/text to centralized systems for processing and improvement. That creates privacy and surveillance risks, which is especially troubling for disabled people who may already be more vulnerable to monitoring and coercive data use. 

So the fact that some accessibility use cases can help does not justify the claim that AI’s welfare effects are dependable overall—because the same unreliability/error-and-bias dynamics that affect other domains can also undermine accessibility, and the privacy harms accompany the accommodations rather than being separable from them.
dialogue_history.target_statement: speech-to-text, text-to-speech, captions, and other assistive AI tools can consistently reduce barriers to communication, learning, and services.

dialogue_history.argument:
AI accessibility benefits may occur in some cases, but they are not reliably “dependable welfare-improving effects.” For accessibility, reliability isn’t just whether an assistive model can sometimes work; it requires stable performance and continued availability over time.

In practice, many AI accessibility tools are vendor-controlled cloud products whose underlying models change (model updates/drift), whose features can be altered or removed, and whose continued access can depend on subscription tiers or service availability. When that happens, accommodations can degrade suddenly or disappear, forcing disabled users to reconfigure workflows or lose access to critical communication/learning support. That kind of instability turns “assistance” into an ongoing barrier rather than a dependable welfare improvement.

Therefore, the target’s claim that AI’s welfare effects are dependable overall—“particularly” via accessibility—doesn’t follow from the existence of some helpful use cases, because the core accessibility requirement (dependable accommodation) is not guaranteed by AI systems operating under these conditions.
dialogue_history.target_statement: AI still has dependable welfare-improving effects in other domains—particularly accessibility for people with disabilities.

dialogue_history.argument:
Artificial Intelligence is not good for society because it systematically weakens critical thinking and independent decision-making—skills that people need to learn, verify claims, and participate effectively in civic and workplace life.

1) AI tools often produce fluent, confident outputs quickly. That creates “outsourced reasoning,” where students, workers, and the public can use AI answers instead of doing the underlying cognitive work (problem solving, source checking, and error detection).

2) When people repeatedly substitute AI’s generated content for their own reasoning, they get less practice at the very abilities required for accuracy: evaluating evidence, spotting gaps, and understanding why an answer is correct.

3) This harms learning outcomes for students and long-term competence for adults: even if AI sometimes gives correct results, the educational value shifts from developing judgment to accepting/patching outputs.

4) In the broader society, weaker critical thinking increases the impact of misinformation and manipulation. People become more likely to treat plausible AI-generated content as trustworthy, which undermines responsible debate and informed decision-making.

Therefore, even if AI can provide convenience, its predictable effect—erosion of critical thinking and judgment—makes it harmful to society rather than “good.”

I don’t accept the idea that AI’s main effect is to push people away from their own reasoning. While some tools may let users copy answers, AI can also be designed and deployed to *promote* critical thinking: for instance, AI tutoring can require learners to choose approaches, answer follow-up questions, and work through explanations and alternatives; workplace copilots can provide drafts alongside evidence, assumptions, and uncertainty, and then ask users to verify or challenge claims rather than accept them blindly. 

So the same “fluency” that concerns the target can be paired with scaffolding that keeps users doing the underlying cognitive work—especially problem solving, source checking, and error detection—rather than outsourcing it.
dialogue_history.target_statement: That creates “outsourced reasoning,” where students, workers, and the public can use AI answers instead of doing the underlying cognitive work (problem solving, source checking, and error detection).

dialogue_history.argument: Even if an AI tool asks follow-ups or tells users to “verify,” the key cognitive shift remains: the system supplies the drafts, explanations, and candidate evidence that people would otherwise have to create and check from independent sources. That means users still rely on AI’s correctness and on the tool’s choice of what counts as evidence. When the model is wrong or misleading, the “verification/challenge” step often becomes another interaction with the same system (e.g., asking it to confirm, rephrase, or “find the source”), rather than independent evaluation. As a result, scaffolding does not reliably preserve critical-thinking practice; it frequently turns reasoning into managing the model’s outputs, which still undermines independent decision-making at the population level.
dialogue_history.target_statement: So the same “fluency” that concerns the target can be paired with scaffolding that keeps users doing the underlying cognitive work—especially problem solving, source checking, and error detection—rather than outsourcing it.

dialogue_history.argument:
AI can support—rather than undermine—critical thinking when it is implemented so that “verification” requires consulting external primary sources and producing user-owned judgments.

Specifically, AI tools can be designed to provide evidence via retrieval of original documents (with quotations/citations) and to restrict answers to what those sources actually support. Then the learner/worker’s task is not to ask the same system to confirm, but to evaluate the cited source(s), compare them to the user’s own interpretation, and show the reasoning steps (e.g., what claim follows from which passage, what would change the conclusion). In education and professional settings, assignments and assessments can also be structured to grade the process of reasoning and source evaluation (or require oral/transparent justification), making “managing outputs” insufficient.

Under such conditions, scaffolding reliably trains judgment: AI provides guidance and organization, while independent evaluation of external evidence remains the basis for the final decision. That directly contradicts the target’s claim that scaffolding frequently turns reasoning into managing the model’s outputs in a way that undermines independent decision-making at the population level.
dialogue_history.target_statement: As a result, scaffolding does not reliably preserve critical-thinking practice; it frequently turns reasoning into managing the model’s outputs, which still undermines independent decision-making at the population level.

dialogue_history.argument:
Even if an AI system displays “quotations/citations,” the evidence is still mediated by the model’s retrieval and extraction layer. In practice, users must rely on the system to (a) find which primary sources are relevant, (b) select which passages to quote or highlight, and (c) format those passages as “what the source actually supports.” That mediation undermines the target’s claim that users truly evaluate external evidence independently and remain in charge of the epistemic basis. 

Because AI systems can produce incorrect or misleading quotes/citations (e.g., inaccurate extraction, out-of-context snippets, or fabricated-looking citations), the user’s “evaluation of the cited source(s)” can become evaluation of AI-presented representations rather than independent verification of the underlying documents. Moreover, many learners/workers lack the time, access, or inclination to check full texts for every claim, so they will tend to treat the AI’s cited passages as authoritative shortcuts. That means scaffolding may change the *workflow* but not the core cognitive dependency: people still outsource the hardest epistemic work—deciding what to trust and why—to the AI’s outputs.

Therefore, AI scaffolding of the sort described cannot be relied on to “reliably train judgment,” and it still functions as outsourced reasoning that weakens critical thinking.
dialogue_history.target_statement: Under such conditions, scaffolding reliably trains judgment: AI provides guidance and organization, while independent evaluation of external evidence remains the basis for the final decision.

dialogue_history.argument:
Mediation by AI retrieval/extraction does not inherently “undermine” independent evaluation. What matters is whether the user can directly inspect the primary evidence that underlies each claim and remain epistemically responsible for what they accept. If an AI provides verbatim, source-anchored passages with precise, checkable location metadata (so users can open the original document and confirm the quoted text), then the AI is functioning like a retrieval/search-and-annotation aid—helpful for finding and organizing evidence, but not a substitute for judgment.

Even if some citations are wrong, the key is that the evidence presented is auditable against the original source; that makes errors detectable and correctable during the learning process rather than turning evaluation into blind trust. Under these design conditions, scaffolding can reliably support judgment by focusing users on interpreting and reasoning from what they can verify in the primary materials—not on outsourcing the epistemic basis to the AI’s output.
dialogue_history.target_statement: That mediation undermines the target’s claim that users truly evaluate external evidence independently and remain in charge of the epistemic basis.

dialogue_history.argument:
Even if an AI provides “verbatim, source-anchored passages with precise, checkable location metadata,” it can still function as a substitute for judgment because it determines the epistemic workflow at the key step: what evidence is surfaced to the user.

Auditable excerpts do not ensure the user can assess *evidential sufficiency*—i.e., whether the presented passage is the best/most relevant support, or whether important contrary or distinguishing evidence was ranked lower, omitted, or never retrieved. In real-world use, users rarely inspect the full universe of relevant primary material, so they cannot reliably tell what AI left out. That means the user’s conclusion depends on AI’s relevance triage and excerpt selection, not only on the literal wording of the quoted snippet.

So scaffolding can reduce the practice of independent evaluation: people still rely on the system’s filtered representation of “what the sources support,” and they can’t correct the epistemic dependency by merely being able to open the displayed excerpt. Therefore, AI scaffolding of this kind cannot reliably train judgment at the population level; it still outsources the core task of deciding what evidence is sufficient and what counterevidence matters.
dialogue_history.target_statement: If an AI provides verbatim, source-anchored passages with precise, checkable location metadata (so users can open the original document and confirm the quoted text), then the AI is functioning like a retrieval/search-and-annotation aid—helpful for finding and organizing evidence, but not a substitute for judgment.

dialogue_history.argument:
AI scaffolding can train independent judgment when it’s designed to make “evidential sufficiency” assessable to the user, not just when it provides a single quotable snippet. Concretely, an AI tutor or workplace assistant can (1) display a *set* of top-retrieved passages (not one excerpt), (2) include key counterevidence or “best arguments for the alternative,” (3) show how the evidence was selected (e.g., the search terms/corpus used and a ranked list of candidate passages/sources), and (4) let the user expand or inspect additional retrieved items. With that transparency, the user can evaluate whether the provided evidence adequately supports the conclusion and can see what evidence would change their mind, rather than being unable to determine what was omitted.

So the key point is that evidential sufficiency depends on the information the system surfaces and how transparently it surfaces it. When AI is engineered to provide a transparent, counterevidence-inclusive evidence set with checkable citations, scaffolding supports learning and judgment rather than substituting for it—making AI beneficial for education and civic/workplace competence.
dialogue_history.target_statement: Auditable excerpts do not ensure the user can assess *evidential sufficiency*—i.e., whether the presented passage is the best/most relevant support, or whether important contrary or distinguishing evidence was ranked lower, omitted, or never retrieved.

dialogue_history.argument:
Evidential sufficiency does not require the user to check every relevant document in the world; it requires the user to assess whether the *best available* supporting and opposing evidence for the specific claim is strong enough to justify acceptance.

AI scaffolding can be designed to make that assessment available to the user by (1) retrieving and presenting multiple top support candidates, and crucially (2) running claim-focused retrieval specifically aimed at finding what would *undermine or falsify* the user’s current hypothesis (i.e., the strongest counterevidence), along with citations to the underlying sources. When the tool surfaces the strongest contrary considerations it can find—and those are checkable—the user can evaluate whether the claim is actually supported “enough” against the best objections in the evidence set.

Under that design, mediation by evidence retrieval does not replace judgment; it structures and trains it. Users learn to decide based on confrontable reasons (the strongest support and counterevidence presented with checkable provenance), which directly supports better reasoning for students and professionals rather than locking them into blind trust.
dialogue_history.target_statement: Auditable excerpts do not ensure the user can assess *evidential sufficiency*—i.e., whether the presented passage is the best/most relevant support, or whether important contrary or distinguishing evidence was ranked lower, omitted, or never retrieved.

dialogue_history.argument:
The target’s key inference relies on the idea that because users typically don’t inspect the full universe of primary material, they cannot reliably assess what evidence is sufficient. But in everyday education, professional practice, and civic reasoning, people routinely form judgments from incomplete information; epistemic sufficiency is about whether the available evidence is strong enough relative to the claim and plausible alternatives—not about whether one has reviewed every relevant document in existence.

AI scaffolding can therefore still support judgment training even when users do not know everything the system left out, because the user can evaluate the presented support and actively test it by requesting additional, contrasting evidence (e.g., targeted retrieval for counterarguments). In that setup, the cognitive task becomes assessing strength and relevance of reasons the user can inspect and challenge, rather than surrendering the epistemic burden to the system’s selection alone.
dialogue_history.target_statement: In real-world use, users rarely inspect the full universe of relevant primary material, so they cannot reliably tell what AI left out.

final_answer:
**Answer:** With the standards set out in the integrated proposal, it **cannot be concluded that AI is unambiguously good for society**. The debate record shows **meaningful, potentially strong benefits** *and* **plausible systematic harms**, but it does **not establish that one side’s case clearly and reliably dominates the other under realistic deployment**—so the verdict is **unresolved**.

## What the debate supports for “AI is GOOD for society” (AG1)
AG1 argues that AI can be socially beneficial if deployed in ways that reliably deliver five kinds of improvements:

1. **Everyday life improvements (convenience/efficiency):**  
   AG1 claims AI personalizes and streamlines common tasks to reduce time/effort.

2. **Health and standard of living via better decisions from complex data:**  
   AG1 argues AI can surface patterns in medical data to support better health choices.

3. **Work/study facilitation:**  
   AG1 says AI helps students and professionals by handling routine, information-heavy, or repetitive parts so people focus on higher-value thinking.

4. **Accessibility for people with disabilities:**  
   AG1 highlights assistive capabilities such as **speech-to-text, text-to-speech, and captions**.

5. **Workplace safety:**  
   AG1 claims AI can identify hazards and flag risks earlier than humans.

AG1 also provides **mitigation mechanisms** against major harms:

- **Privacy risks (mitigation):** reduce personal-data collection using **on-device processing, anonymization, and privacy-preserving learning**.
- **Economic disruption (mitigation):** productivity gains plus **reskilling and job-transition supports** to convert displaced tasks into new work.
- **Safety/health error and bias (mitigation):** **rigorous testing, calibrated thresholds, uncertainty handling, continuous monitoring, human-in-the-loop**; plus **bias auditing and fairness-aware training/evaluation**.
- **Critical thinking concerns (mitigation):** use “scaffolding” that doesn’t outsource reasoning—e.g., tutors/coplots that require user engagement, provide **evidence with citations**, and present **counterevidence** and transparent retrieval so users evaluate sufficiency.

## What the debate supports for “AI is NOT GOOD for society” (AG2)
AG2 argues AI is harmful in a way that is **systematic and predictable**, especially under real use:

1. **Economic well-being harms (automation/data-driven models):**  
   AG2 claims AI can disrupt livelihoods and weaken many workers and small businesses.

2. **Undermining critical thinking (“outsourced reasoning”):**  
   AG2 argues AI produces fluent, confident outputs; people substitute AI drafts for problem-solving and source checking; this erodes learning and adult competence and makes misinformation/manipulation more effective.

3. **Racial harm via repeated/exacerbated bias:**  
   AG2 contends that AI can replicate and exacerbate racism, particularly through data and performance disparities.

4. **Dangerous privacy risks:**  
   AG2 emphasizes privacy harms at scale: misuse, excessive surveillance, leakage—especially through deployment practices that require large data collection.

AG2’s responses also directly challenge AG1’s mitigation strategies:

- **Safety/health reliability challenged:**  
  AG2 argues AI is probabilistic pattern-matching and can produce **false negatives/false positives**; moreover health/safety data reflects inequalities, so harms can be disproportionately distributed.
- **Accessibility reliability challenged:**  
  Even assistive tools can misrecognize accents/voices. Also, many are vendor-controlled cloud products with **model drift**, feature changes, removal, subscription dependence—creating instability. AG2 adds that such systems often rely on collecting/transmitting voice/text, worsening surveillance risk for disabled users.
- **Critical thinking mitigation challenged:**  
  AG2 argues that even when systems show citations, evidence is still mediated by AI retrieval/extraction; users may not evaluate sufficiency because the system decides what to surface or omit; and “verification” can become another interaction with the same system rather than independent evaluation.

## Why the final verdict is **UNRESOLVED** under the integrated proposal
The integrated proposal says:

- Treat deployment as **GOOD** only if evidence indicates the benefits are **reliable** and the predictable systematic harms (especially critical thinking erosion, learning/competence decline, privacy risks, racism, and economic harm) are **not simultaneously likely to be substantial**.
- Treat deployment as **NOT GOOD** if evidence indicates those systematic harms are **likely substantial**, especially with at least one additional harm (privacy, racism, or significant economic harm).
- If **neither side’s showing clearly dominates**, leave the verdict **unresolved**.

In the provided record, both sides offer **mechanisms** and **counterarguments**, but the discussion does **not provide decisive comparative evidence** that either:
- AG1’s safeguards will *consistently* prevent the systematic harms at realistic scale, **or**
- AG2’s alleged failure modes will be *substantial enough* to swamp the benefits across deployments.

So, using the integrated proposal’s decision rule, the correct conclusion is: **unresolved**.

## What remains genuinely unresolved (the sticking points)
The debate does not settle these key questions:

1. **Net reliability across real-world deployment:**  
   Whether the kinds of “reliably improves” AG1 claims (health/safety/assistive functioning and general welfare improvement) hold under real conditions, given AG2’s emphasis on false positives/negatives, data inequality, and operational drift.

2. **Whether “scaffolding with citations/counterevidence” truly preserves independent judgment at population scale:**  
   AG1 argues careful design enables auditable, user-directed evaluation; AG2 argues mediation and evidence triage still shift epistemic dependency and reduce critical-thinking practice.

3. **Privacy and surveillance risks in common deployment models:**  
   Whether mitigations (on-device, anonymization, privacy-preserving learning) are typically achievable and sufficient given practical product incentives and real-world data practices.

4. **Accessibility stability for disabled users:**  
   Whether assistive systems can remain dependable over time (accounting for model updates, feature removal, subscription/service dependence) and whether voice/text processing can be made safe enough.

---

### Bottom line
**Artificial Intelligence might be good for society under constrained, well-governed conditions, but the debate does not establish that those conditions reliably prevent the systematic harms AG2 emphasizes. Therefore, the overall verdict—per the integrated proposal—is **unresolved** rather than confidently “yes” or “no.”**
integrated_rules:
Treat claims about AI as supporting “AI is good for society” only if the argument shows (reliably, across real-world use) that AI does *all* of the following: (1) makes everyday life more enjoyable and convenient by personalizing/streamlining common tasks in ways that reduce time and effort; (2) improves health and standard of living by supporting better decisions in health contexts (e.g., surfacing patterns in complex medical/health data) leading to better health outcomes; (3) makes work easier for students and professionals by handling routine, information-heavy, or repetitive parts of learning/work so people can focus on higher-value thinking; (4) expands accessibility for people with disabilities via assistive capabilities (e.g., speech-to-text, text-to-speech, captions) that lower barriers to communication/learning/services; and (5) improves workplace safety by identifying hazards and flagging risks earlier than humans typically would.

Treat claims as supporting “AI is not good/harmful for society” when the argument shows the effects are *systematic/predictable* in practice and include (at a comparable or greater real-world magnitude and likelihood, and not effectively mitigated): (a) outsourced reasoning that systematically weakens critical thinking and independent decision-making—people substitute fluent, confident AI outputs for underlying problem-solving, source checking, and error detection—thereby reducing practice with evaluating evidence, harming learning outcomes and long-term competence (even if some AI outputs are correct), and increasing the impact of misinformation/manipulation because people treat plausible AI-generated content as trustworthy; and (b) harms to economic well-being of many people and businesses, plus one or more of: (c) harming racial minorities by repeating/exacerbating racism, and (d) posing dangerous privacy risks.

If an argument establishes both the pro-benefits (1–5) and the con-harms with similarly strong evidence of magnitude/likelihood and without adequate mitigation, then the overall “good vs not good” assessment is unresolved rather than decided by either side’s presence alone.
integrated_proposal: For a proposed AI deployment, treat it as GOOD for society if the best available evidence indicates (1) it reliably improves everyday life by personalizing and streamlining common tasks to reduce time/effort, (2) it can improve health and standard of living by supporting better decisions from complex information (e.g., surfacing patterns in medical data), (3) it makes work easier for students and professionals by handling routine, information-heavy, or repetitive components so people can focus on higher-value thinking, (4) it expands accessibility for people with disabilities through assistive capabilities such as speech-to-text/text-to-speech and captions that lower communication/learning/service barriers, and (5) it improves workplace safety by identifying hazards/monitoring conditions and flagging risks earlier than humans; and it does NOT simultaneously show a predictable, systematic pattern of (a) weakening critical thinking and independent decision-making via “outsourced reasoning” (fluent, confident outputs substituting for underlying problem solving and source checking), (b) worsening learning outcomes for students and long-term competence for adults and thereby increasing vulnerability to misinformation/manipulation, (c) dangerous privacy risks, (d) harming racial minorities by repeating or exacerbating racism, and (e) harming the economic well-being of many people and businesses. Treat it as NOT GOOD (harmful) if the evidence instead indicates that these predictable, systematic harms—especially erosion of critical thinking/judgment under real use—are likely to be substantial (and at least one of the additional harms—dangerous privacy risks, exacerbated racism toward racial minorities, or significant economic harm to many people/businesses—also occurs). If credible evidence supports both strong reliable benefits and strong predictable systematic harms, compare their likelihood and magnitude under realistic deployment; if neither side’s showing clearly dominates, leave the verdict unresolved.
